items.prose: On a 120-day window, regressing $y$ on $x$ gives a hedge ratio of 1.50, with $R^2 = 0.75$.
items.question: What hedge ratio does regressing $x$ on $y$ and inverting give? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The inverted ratio is the direct one divided by $R^2$.

byKey.same: You assumed the two directions agree. They do only when $R^2 = 1$.

explain.text: The two slopes multiply to $R^2$, so $1/\hat\beta_{x|y} = \hat\beta_{y|x}/R^2 = 1.50/0.75 = 2.00$. A loose window gives very different hedges by direction.

items.prose: A spread closes at £2.10. Over the last 60 days, today included, its mean is £0.30 and its sample sd is £0.60.
items.question: What is today's rolling z-score? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Correct. 3.00: past the entry line, short of the stop at 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the mean, then divide by the sd.

byKey.nomean: You divided £2.10 by £0.60 without subtracting the mean.
byKey.pounds: That is the distance in pounds. Divide by the sd.

explain.text: $(2.10 - 0.30)/0.60 = 3.00$ sds above the 60-day mean. Both the mean and the sd come from days up to today.

items.prose: The regression $\Delta s_t = a + b\,s_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ on a stationary spread gives $b = -0.07$.
items.question: What is the half-life in days? Give 2 decimal places.

byKey.guide: You used $1/0.07$, the rough guide to the mean-reversion time. The half-life uses logs.
byKey.lin: You assumed a straight-line fall of 7% a day to half. The decay compounds.

explain.text: $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.93 = -0.6931/-0.0726 = 9.55$ days. In continuous time, $\kappa = -\ln 0.93 = 0.0726$ a day and $h = \ln 2/\kappa$.

items.prose: Johansen on four sector ETFs gives the trace statistics in the table, from $r = 0$ down, with their 95% critical values.
items.question: What is the cointegration rank, and how many common trends are there?

options.text: Rank 2, so two common trends
Rank 4: the last row rejects
options.why: The reading stops at $r \le 2$, where 9.1 < 15.5. The last row is never reached.

options.text: Rank 1: stop at the first rejection
options.why: A rejection means "more than this". Move down until a row fails to reject.

options.text: Rank 2, so three common trends

feedback.correct: Correct. Reject, reject, then stop: rank 2 and $4 - 2 = 2$ trends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read from the top and stop at the first failure to reject.

explain.text: 61.2 > 47.9 and 33.9 > 29.8 reject; 9.1 < 15.5 stops the reading. Rank 2 of 4 series leaves 2 common trends.

items.prose: Three ways to build the z-score a backtest trades on, for a pair over 1,500 days.
items.question: Which one uses only information available at each day's close?

options.text: Each day, fit $y$ on $x$ over the last 250 days and divide today's residual by that window's residual sd
Fit $y$ on $x$ once on all 1,500 days, then z-score the residual with its full-sample mean and sd
options.why: The fit, the mean and the sd all use days after each signal. In lesson 6's comparison it lifted the Sharpe from 1.12 to 1.65.

options.text: Fit $\beta$ on all 1,500 days, then use a trailing 60-day mean and sd of that residual
options.why: The trailing window is honest, but $\beta$ itself was fitted with future prices.

options.text: Use a centred 60-day window, 30 days either side of each day
options.why: Half of a centred window is the future.

feedback.correct: Correct. Every input to day $t$'s z comes from days up to $t$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every estimate, the hedge ratio included, for future days.

explain.text: Only the rolling regression keeps $\alpha$, $\beta$ and the sd inside each day's past. A full-sample $\beta$ leaks the future even when the mean and sd are trailing.

items.prose: A spread's half-life is 48 days, and its 95% interval runs from 19 days to infinity. Its Engle-Granger $p$ is 0.31.
items.question: What should a desk conclude?

options.text: There is no evidence the spread reverts at all; the half-life is not usable
It reverts slowly, in about 48 days
options.why: With $p = 0.31$ the spread may be a random walk. The open interval says the same.

options.text: Use the short end: it may revert in 19 days
options.why: Picking the friendliest end of an interval is wishful. The long end is infinite.

options.text: Trade it at half size until the estimate settles
options.why: Size is not the issue: the test says there may be nothing to trade.

feedback.correct: Correct. Test first; a half-life needs a stationary spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the test and the open end of the interval together.

explain.text: $p = 0.31$ does not reject a unit root, and $b + 1.96\,\text{se} \ge 0$ puts the long end at infinity. Lesson 7's pair A gave a finite 121.6 days on a random walk the same way.

items.prose: A VECM for two gaps gives series A the speeds $\alpha_{A} = (-0.10, 0.05)$ on $(z_1, z_2)$. Yesterday $z_1 = 1.5$ and $z_2 = -2.0$.
items.question: What is A's expected change today? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Correct. −0.25: both gaps push A down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each gap by its speed and add both.

byKey.sign: You added $+0.10$ for the second term. $0.05 \times (-2.0) = -0.10$.

explain.text: $-0.10 \times 1.5 = -0.15$ and $0.05 \times (-2.0) = -0.10$, so A is expected to move −0.25. Each $\alpha$ is a speed of adjustment, the many-series version of a half-life's $b$.

items.prose: Two spreads, both cointegrated: P with a half-life of 4 days, Q with a half-life of 60 days. A desk z-scores both with the same trailing 20-day window.
items.question: What goes wrong for Q?

options.text: Its 20-day window spans a third of one half-life, so the window mean chases the spread
Nothing for Q; the problem is P
options.why: P's swings fit easily in 20 days. Q's slow swings do not: the window's mean follows them.

options.text: Q's z is NaN for the first 60 days
options.why: The NaN run is set by the window, 19 days for both.

options.text: The 20-day window leaks the future
options.why: A trailing window has no look-ahead, whatever its length.

feedback.correct: Correct. Match the window to the half-life.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 20 days with each half-life.

explain.text: In 20 days Q closes only a fifth of a gap, while the window's mean drifts with the spread. A window of a few half-lives fits P; Q would need hundreds of days. Lesson 7's rule of thumb ties window to half-life.

items.prose: On 250 days of pair C, total least squares gives 2.06 with both prices in pounds. With $y$ in pence, divided back to pounds, it gives 2.13.
items.question: Why did rescaling $y$ change the TLS hedge ratio?

options.text: TLS measures perpendicular distance, which mixes the two axes' units; in pence $y$'s gaps dominate
It should not; one of the two is a rounding error
options.why: The change, 2.06 to 2.13, is far beyond rounding. TLS is not unit-free.

options.text: Because TLS is really OLS of $y$ on $x$
options.why: OLS of $y$ on $x$ gives 1.80 and does not change with units. TLS moves towards the $x$ on $y$ fit.

options.text: Because the 250 days were redrawn
options.why: The same 250 days were used. Only the units changed.

feedback.correct: Correct. TLS depends on the units, unlike either OLS slope.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a perpendicular distance means when the axes have different units.

explain.text: In pence, $y$ has 10,000 times the variance. The first principal component then lines up with the $x$ on $y$ fit, 2.13. Least squares slopes do not depend on units; TLS does.
